name: Absinthe Drip
description: Absinthe, a slotted spoon, a sugar cube and iced water dripped over it until the glass clouds green-white. The ritual is most of the drink.
glassware: Absinthe glass with a slotted spoon
funFact: The louche — the cloud that forms as water hits — happens because the anise oils are soluble in alcohol but not water; if your absinthe does not louche, it is coloured spirit, not absinthe.

steps: Pour the absinthe into an absinthe glass or a small tumbler.
Rest a slotted spoon across the rim and set the sugar cube on it.
Drip iced water very slowly over the sugar cube so it dissolves into the absinthe.
Keep dripping until the drink turns opaque — roughly three to five parts water to one of absinthe.
Stir once and drink at room temperature.

name: Blue Lagoon
description: Vodka, blue curaçao and lemonade — electric blue, faintly ridiculous, and genuinely refreshing if you make it with real lemon.
funFact: Created at Harry's New York Bar in Paris in the 1960s — the same bar credited with the Bloody Mary, the Sidecar and the French 75, and responsible for a suspicious share of the twentieth century's drinking.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the vodka, blue curaçao and lemon juice.
Top with lemonade and stir once.
Garnish with a lemon wheel and a cherry.

name: Champs-Élysées
description: Cognac, Chartreuse and lemon — a Sidecar that went to the monastery and came back with opinions about herbs.
funFact: It appears in Harry Craddock's 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book, and is one of the few classics where green Chartreuse plays a supporting role rather than dominating everything it touches.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and discard it.

name: Communard
description: The Kir's red half-brother: red Burgundy with cassis, named for the Paris Commune and considerably more serious about itself.
funFact: Also called a Cardinal, for the colour of a cardinal's robes — the two names carry opposite politics for exactly the same drink.

steps: Pour the crème de cassis into a wine glass.
Add the cold red wine.
Stir gently and serve.
Keep the wine light — a heavy red buries the cassis.

name: Kir
description: White Burgundy with a measure of blackcurrant liqueur. Invented to make thin wine drinkable and now ordered on its own merits.
funFact: Named for Canon Félix Kir, mayor of Dijon after the war, who served it at official receptions to promote two local products at once — the sharp Aligoté grape and Dijon's cassis.

steps: Pour the crème de cassis into the bottom of a wine glass.
Top with cold dry white wine.
Stir once, gently, to combine.
Serve without ice or garnish.

name: Mauresque
description: Pastis softened with orgeat until it turns milky and almond-sweet. The gentlest member of the Marseille colour family.
funFact: The name means 'Moorish', a nod to the almond-and-orange-flower orgeat that came into Provence through North African and Spanish trade.

steps: Pour the pastis and orgeat into a tumbler.
Top slowly with cold water until the drink turns opaque and pale.
Stir once to combine.
Add ice last if you want it colder.

name: Monaco
description: Lager, lemonade and grenadine — pink, low-proof and what half of France orders on a café terrace in July.
funFact: It sits in a French family of low-proof beer mixes: the Panaché is beer and lemonade, the Tango uses grenadine with more beer, and the Monaco is the one with all three.

steps: Pour the grenadine into the bottom of the glass.
Add the lemonade.
Top slowly with the lager, tilting the glass to control the head.
Stir once, very gently, to bring the pink through.

name: Monkey Gland
description: Gin, orange juice, grenadine and absinthe, named after a genuinely alarming 1920s medical procedure.
funFact: It is named for Serge Voronoff, a surgeon who grafted monkey testicle tissue onto human patients as a rejuvenation treatment; Harry MacElhone named the drink while the story was still in the papers.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with an orange twist.

name: Perroquet
description: Pastis turned green with mint syrup — the 'parrot', one of a whole southern French family named for their colours.
funFact: The southern French colour code is fixed: mint makes a Perroquet, grenadine a Tomate, orgeat a Mauresque, and lemon syrup a Canari — order by colour and every bar from Nice to Sète understands you.

steps: Pour the pastis and mint syrup into a tall tumbler.
Add cold water slowly and watch the drink go cloudy and green.
Stir once.
Add ice only after the water — ice first will make the pastis seize.

name: Picon Bière
description: A shot of bitter orange Picon in the bottom of a beer glass. Eastern France's default order, and an acquired taste worth acquiring.
funFact: Amer Picon was created in Algeria in 1837 as a quinine tonic for French soldiers; its modern formulation is much weaker than the original, which is why old cocktail books calling for Picon rarely taste right today.

steps: Pour the Picon into the bottom of a beer glass.
Fill slowly with cold lager, letting the beer mix it as it goes.
Do not stir — the pour does the work.
Serve with no garnish.

name: Rose
description: Dry vermouth, kirsch and a whisper of raspberry, stirred pale pink. The Paris cocktail the Prohibition Americans took home with them.
funFact: Created around 1920 by Johnny Mitta at the Chatham Hotel bar in Paris, and one of the most-ordered cocktails in the city between the wars before it vanished almost entirely.

steps: Combine the vermouth, kirsch and raspberry syrup in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 25 seconds until well chilled.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a cherry.

name: Tomate
description: Pastis stained red with grenadine. No tomato involved — the name is purely about what it looks like in the glass.
funFact: In Provençal bars the pastis, the syrup and a jug of cold water arrive separately, and diluting it yourself is part of the ritual — roughly five parts water to one of pastis.

steps: Pour the pastis and grenadine into a tumbler.
Add cold water slowly until the drink louches to a cloudy pink-red.
Stir once.
Serve with a jug of extra water on the side.

name: Hot Whiskey
description: Irish whiskey, boiling water, sugar, a lemon studded with cloves. Prescribed for colds, drunk for weather, effective for both.
funFact: Irish pubs serve it in a glass with a metal spoon left in — not for stirring, but to conduct heat away from the glass so it does not crack when the boiling water hits.

steps: Stud the lemon slice with the cloves and drop it into a heatproof glass.
Add the sugar and the whiskey.
Put a metal spoon in the glass, then pour in the boiling water.
Stir until the sugar dissolves and leave for a minute before drinking.

name: Irish Flag
description: Green, white and orange, layered in that order: crème de menthe, Irish cream, orange liqueur. Structurally demanding, spiritually simple.
funFact: The layering only holds if you pour in descending sugar density — and the Irish cream will curdle if it touches anything acidic, which is why the orange liqueur goes on top and never underneath.

steps: Pour the crème de menthe into the bottom of a shot glass.
Float the Irish cream over the back of a barspoon held against the glass.
Float the Grand Marnier the same way to finish the flag.
Serve immediately and drink in one.

name: Angel Face
description: Equal parts gin, apricot brandy and calvados. Three spirits, no citrus, and a name that undersells it considerably.
funFact: It appears in the 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book with no story attached — one of many equal-parts drinks from that era that survive on balance alone.

steps: Add all three spirits to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with an apple slice or a lemon twist.

name: Atholl Brose
description: Oatmeal steeped in water, strained, then stirred with honey, cream and whisky. A Highland recipe old enough to have won a battle.
funFact: Legend holds that the Earl of Atholl put down a Highland rebellion in 1475 by filling his enemy's well with the mixture and capturing him while he was drinking it.

steps: Soak the oatmeal in the water for at least six hours, then strain through muslin, pressing to extract the creamy liquid.
Discard the oats and stir the honey into the oat liquid until dissolved.
Whisk in the whisky.
Fold in the lightly whipped cream just before serving.
Serve chilled in small glasses; it keeps a couple of days in the fridge.

name: Black Velvet
description: Stout and champagne, poured half and half so the black sits under the gold. Invented for a funeral and never quite shook the mood.
funFact: Created at Brooks's Club in London in 1861 after Prince Albert's death, when the steward decided even the champagne should be in mourning.

ingredients.item: Champagne or dry sparkling wine, chilled

steps: Chill both the stout and the champagne well.
Pour the stout into a tall glass and let the head settle.
Pour the champagne slowly over the back of a spoon to layer it on top.
Serve immediately, while the two are still separate.

name: Buck's Fizz
description: Two parts champagne to one part orange juice — the older, stronger, more London answer to the Mimosa, and the two have been arguing ever since.
funFact: Created at the Buck's Club in Mayfair in 1921 by barman Malachy McGarry, three years before the Mimosa appeared at the Ritz Paris — the difference is the ratio, and Londoners will tell you so.

ingredients.item: Champagne or dry sparkling wine, chilled

steps: Chill both the champagne and the orange juice thoroughly.
Pour the orange juice into a flute first.
Top slowly with champagne, tilting the glass to preserve the bubbles.
Do not stir — the pour mixes it.

name: John Collins
description: The Tom Collins made with whiskey instead of gin — lemon, sugar, soda, tall and cold. The original of the family, depending who you ask.
funFact: John Collins was the head waiter at Limmer's Hotel in London in the early 1800s; the gin version took his colleague's name, and the two have been confused with each other ever since.

steps: Shake the whiskey, lemon juice and sugar syrup with ice.
Strain into a Collins glass filled with fresh ice.
Top with cold soda water.
Stir once and garnish with a lemon wheel and a cherry.

name: Paradise
description: Gin, apricot brandy and orange juice. Simple, apricot-forward and one of the few Savoy-era drinks that needs no adjustment at all.
funFact: Apricot brandy in these recipes means an apricot liqueur, not a distilled eau-de-vie — a distinction that ruins the drink for anyone who buys the wrong bottle.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with an orange twist.

name: Pink Gin
description: Navy strength gin stained pink with Angostura and nothing else. Two ingredients, no ice, no apology.
funFact: Angostura was issued to Royal Navy officers as a stomach remedy; mixing it into the gin ration was the medicinal excuse that turned into an institution, and Plymouth Gin still trades on the association.

steps: Dash the Angostura into a chilled coupe and roll it around to coat the inside.
Discard any excess bitters, or leave them in for a stronger version.
Stir the gin over ice for 20 seconds, or serve it neat and cold from the freezer.
Strain into the coated coupe and serve without garnish.

name: Russian Spring Punch
description: Dick Bradsell's long, fizzing sour: vodka, crème de cassis, lemon and champagne over crushed ice. Modern London's house punch.
funFact: Bradsell — who also gave the world the Espresso Martini and the Bramble — created it in the 1980s at the Soho Brasserie, and it remains the drink London bartenders make when they want to show off without saying so.

steps: Shake the vodka, cassis, lemon juice and sugar syrup with ice.
Strain into a tall glass packed with crushed ice.
Top with champagne and stir gently once.
Add more crushed ice to cap the glass and garnish with berries and a lemon slice.
recipe.garnish: Fresh berries and a lemon slice

name: Snakebite
description: Lager and cider, half and half, with a shot of blackcurrant if you want it purple. The most-refused drink in British pubs.
funFact: Many British pubs refuse to serve it, citing an urban myth about the mix being unusually intoxicating — the real reason is that it is cheap, strong and popular with students.

steps: Pour the cider into a pint glass first.
Add the lager slowly at an angle to keep the foam down.
Add a dash of blackcurrant cordial if making a Snakebite and Black.
Do not stir.

name: Snowball
description: Advocaat and lemonade with a squeeze of lime — a yellow, foamy relic of the British Christmas drinks trolley that refuses to die.
funFact: Advocaat is Dutch, but the Snowball is entirely British — a 1960s Christmas fixture that has been ironically revived so many times it is now simply back.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the advocaat and lime cordial.
Top with lemonade and stir briskly until the drink foams pale yellow.
Garnish with a maraschino cherry and, if you are committing to it, a slice of orange.

name: Treacle
description: An Old Fashioned with a float of apple juice on top. Bradsell again, and one of the few modern riffs the classicists never argued with.
funFact: Bradsell built it at the Player in Soho as a rum Old Fashioned, then floated cloudy apple juice over the top — the apple reads as freshness on the nose and disappears entirely by the second sip.

steps: Stir the rum, sugar syrup and bitters over ice until chilled and lightly diluted.
Strain over one large ice cube in a rocks glass.
Float the apple juice gently over the top so it sits as a distinct layer.
Express an orange twist over the surface and drop it in.

name: Whisky Mac
description: Scotch and green ginger wine, in equal measure, no ice. The drink Scotland reaches for when the weather turns properly hostile.
funFact: Named for Colonel Hector Macdonald, and traditionally made with Stone's Ginger Wine — a British fortified ginger wine that has been made since 1740 and exists almost solely for this purpose.

steps: Pour the Scotch and the ginger wine into a small tumbler.
Stir briefly to combine.
Serve at room temperature — ice is considered a mistake.
Drink beside something warm.

name: White Lady
description: Gin, triple sec and lemon, shaken with egg white to a dense pale foam. The Sidecar's gin cousin, and quietly one of the best.
funFact: Harry MacElhone first made it with crème de menthe in 1919, then rebuilt it with gin at Harry's New York Bar in Paris in 1929 — the second version is the one that survived.

steps: Dry-shake all the ingredients without ice for 15 seconds to build the foam.
Add ice and shake hard again for 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Let the foam settle before garnishing with a lemon twist.

name: Wibble
description: Gin, sloe gin, grapefruit and lemon — pink, brambly and named for what it does to your legs, not your speech.
funFact: Dick Bradsell created it at The Player and said the name came from the fact that 'it makes you wibble, not wobble' — sloe gin was deeply unfashionable at the time and the drink helped rescue it.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lemon twist.
